ratings.rationale: Modification of existing observables is tampering, not spoofing. False measurement inputs can produce displaced positions. False-data-injection literature supports the general mechanism, but only by analogy. W2 enables L3 detection; W3 permits undetected displacement.
ratings.issue: The cited power-grid literature establishes an analogous estimation vulnerability, not feasibility in satellite MLAT. A2.4 is the relevant transport asset.

ratings.rationale: Impersonating a reporting node fabricates observations attributable to a legitimate source. Satellite downlink overshadowing provides relevant experimental support, but not in this MLAT architecture. Fabricated reports can create deceptive tracks or distort genuine tracks.
ratings.issue: Substantial overlap with T2.09. Distinction should be explicitly restricted to node identity impersonation rather than generic downlink injection.

ratings.rationale: Selective delay and reordering tamper with report timing and association. This differs from PTP manipulation because the underlying clock need not change. Network delay research supports the general mechanism; L3 may detect stale or inconsistent measurements.
ratings.issue: The mechanism conflates delay, reordering and modification, which have different effects. The cited satellite overshadowing work does not independently establish selective report-delay attacks.

ratings.rationale: Selective loss of geometrically valuable observations is denial-oriented and degrades observability. As explicitly scoped, its principal role is enabling other errors to evade detection, not independently producing a specified target-report consequence. HDOP changes are observable at L3.
ratings.issue: The enabler designation is appropriate only if independent regional denial is excluded. Evidence from LEO network simulation does not establish the specific MLAT geometry effect.

ratings.rationale: Crosslink disruption removes report-relay capacity and can reduce surveillance coverage. This is a conventional availability threat, but the record explicitly acknowledges no published mechanism against the relevant terminals. Link-loss monitoring should reveal disruption.
ratings.issue: Valid postulated threat, not demonstrated attack capability. Distinguish physical crosslink disruption from congestion and selective report dropping in T2.04.

ratings.rationale: Asymmetric delay changes the computed clock reference even with authenticated messages, satisfying the tau invariance test. PTP/NTP research supports the timing mechanism. W2 permits downstream detection; W3 permits an undetected clock-induced position error.
ratings.issue: The cited terrestrial timing results are analogue evidence. The record should distinguish clock-offset manipulation from ordinary report latency.

ratings.rationale: Fabricated or replayed timing messages impersonate legitimate time-transfer information. Unlike T2.06, sound authentication prevents the stated mechanism, so this is not tau under the invariance test. Clock displacement remains the downstream consequence.
ratings.issue: The authentication assumption needs clarification regarding replay protection, freshness and endpoint compromise. Otherwise this remains distinct from authenticated-message delay in T2.06.

ratings.rationale: Passive interception is information disclosure, not direct report manipulation. The maritime VSAT research provides relevant analogue evidence for satellite communication exposure. Consumer reception capability lowers the adversary threshold. Passive collection may enable subsequent injection.
ratings.issue: Confidentiality depends on actual encryption and traffic protection, which are unspecified. Distinguish public broadcast observables from genuinely confidential backhaul traffic.

ratings.rationale: Injection accepted as genuine reporting fabricates observations and can create ghost targets. Satellite downlink overshadowing supports the general possibility, but the ADS-C reference does not establish this exact MLAT downlink scenario. Integrity checks may expose inconsistencies.
ratings.issue: Overlaps T2.02. The record does not establish whether the attacker can overcome link authentication, source validation or report provenance checks.

ratings.rationale: Passive command-channel interception discloses control-path information and potentially credentials or configuration. It does not itself modify satellite behaviour. The evidence is indirect and analogue; successful exploitation depends on actual confidentiality protections.
ratings.issue: The record conflates command confidentiality with key disclosure. Encrypted command traffic may expose metadata without revealing command content or credentials.

ratings.rationale: Accepted forged commands provide control-path privilege over satellite functions and permit configuration or software modification. Satellite experimental security research supports the general capability on hardware. Consequences can extend across the constellation; operational monitoring may reveal changes.
ratings.issue: Depends on the separate key-disclosure or authentication-weakness precondition. The record should distinguish command acceptance from subsequent platform compromise and operational effects.

ratings.rationale: Compromising network infrastructure provides elevated control over report transport, enabling tampering and denial. SATCOM terminal vulnerabilities and government advisories support the general exposure, but not necessarily this architecture. Effects may propagate across several footprints.
ratings.issue: Entry layer is L2, but the threat spans infrastructure potentially owned by L1 and L3. Specify the affected device classes and distinguish compromise from subsequent traffic manipulation.

missing_threats.title: Inter-satellite-link confidentiality failure
missing_threats.why: ISL traffic interception and disclosure are not separately covered by the downlink/backhaul interception record.

missing_threats.title: Report replay and freshness failure
missing_threats.why: Replay of previously valid observable reports is distinct from fabrication, field modification and selective delay.

missing_threats.title: Downlink jamming and interference
missing_threats.why: RF availability disruption is not explicitly distinguished from network-device compromise or crosslink denial.

missing_threats.title: Telecommand authentication downgrade
missing_threats.why: Negotiation or fallback weaknesses could undermine command authentication without requiring prior key disclosure.

missing_threats.title: Report provenance and integrity failure
missing_threats.why: Missing end-to-end integrity and provenance protection across multiple relay stages deserves explicit treatment.

rubric_ambiguities: The enabler definition conflicts with Damage scoring when report dropping independently degrades geometry but primarily facilitates another threat.
The relationship between W2/W3 and threats other than single-satellite timing bias is not formally specified.
Evidence levels do not clearly distinguish experimental demonstration on satellite hardware from simulation or laboratory emulation.
The tier rubric does not explicitly map AC4 timing adversaries and AC5 link adversaries to individual capability tiers.
Affected users may mean aircraft, ATM facilities or geographic coverage; the rubric mixes these interpretations.
batch_comments.overall: The batch covers important L2 confidentiality, integrity, availability and timing risks. The strongest conceptual distinction is authenticated-message delay versus forged timing messages. Several records overlap, particularly T2.02/T2.09 and T2.04/T2.05. Most supporting evidence is analogue rather than LEO-MLAT-specific. The model should distinguish demonstrated mechanisms from architectural extrapolations and explicitly address replay, provenance and end-to-end protection.
